_about: LanWatch remediation (advice) knowledge base. One article per piece of advice, referred to by id from ports.json and app/services/findings.py. ADVICE ONLY: LanWatch never changes any device itself. difficulty: easy | medium | advanced.

disable_telnet.title: Turn off Telnet
disable_telnet.why: Telnet sends passwords without encryption. Anyone on your network could read them and take control of the device.
steps: Find out which device it is (name, maker and address are shown in LanWatch).
Open the device's settings page or app. For routers, cameras and printers this is usually its address typed into a web browser.
Look for 'Telnet', 'Remote access', 'Remote management' or 'Advanced > Services', and switch Telnet off.
If there is no option to switch it off, update the device's software (firmware). If it still can't be switched off, ask the maker or consider replacing the device.

disable_ftp.title: Turn off FTP or switch to a secure option
disable_ftp.why: FTP sends passwords and files without encryption, so they can be read by others on your network.
steps: Open the device's settings page or app (often network storage or a printer).
Look for 'FTP', 'File services' or 'File transfer' and switch FTP off if you don't use it.
If you need file transfer, choose 'SFTP' or 'FTPS' (the encrypted versions) if the device offers them.

strong_device_passwords.title: Use a strong, unique password on the device
strong_device_passwords.why: A device's settings page or login is only as safe as its password. Default and simple passwords are the first thing attackers try.
steps: Open the device's settings page or app and find 'Administrator', 'Admin password' or 'Account'.
If the password is still the one printed on the device or in its manual, change it.
Use a long password you don't use anywhere else (a password manager makes this easy).

router_default_password.title: Check your router's admin password isn't the default
router_default_password.why: Your router controls your whole network. Its settings page is reachable from every device at home, and default admin passwords are widely known. LanWatch never tries passwords itself: this is a reminder to check.
steps: Type your router's address (shown in LanWatch) into a web browser to open its settings page.
Log in. If the admin password is the one on the sticker or in the manual (or something like 'admin'), change it.
Look for 'Administration', 'System' or 'Management', and set a long, unique password.
This is the admin password for the router's settings, not the Wi-Fi password, although changing a default Wi-Fi password is also a good idea.

router_https_admin.title: Use the encrypted (HTTPS) settings page on your router
router_https_admin.why: Your router's settings page is not encrypted, so your admin password could be read by another device on your network while you log in.
steps: Open your router's settings page and look for 'HTTPS', 'Secure management' or 'Local management'.
Switch on HTTPS (encrypted) access if it is available, and switch off plain HTTP if you can.
If there is no such option, update the router's software (firmware), and only log in to it from devices you trust.

disable_upnp.title: Consider turning off UPnP on your router
disable_upnp.why: UPnP lets any device at home open connections from the internet without asking you. It is convenient for games and video calls, but a compromised device could misuse it.
steps: Open your router's settings page and look for 'UPnP' (often under 'Advanced', 'NAT' or 'Network').
Switch it off if you don't need it.
If a game console or app stops working afterwards, you can switch it back on, or set up only the specific connection it needs ('port forwarding').

review_file_sharing.title: Check what this device is sharing
review_file_sharing.why: File sharing is normal on computers and network storage, but shared folders should need a password and only contain what you mean to share.
steps: On Windows: Settings > Network & internet > Advanced network settings > Advanced sharing settings. Turn off file and printer sharing on networks you don't trust.
On network storage: open its app or settings page and check each shared folder has a password and isn't open to 'everyone' or 'guest'.
On a device that shouldn't share files at all (a TV or camera, for example), look for a 'file sharing' or 'SMB' option and turn it off.

review_remote_desktop.title: Make sure remote screen control is meant to be on
review_remote_desktop.why: Remote Desktop and VNC let someone control this device's screen. If you don't use them, they are an unnecessary way in; if you do, they need a strong password.
steps: If you don't use remote control: on Windows go to Settings > System > Remote Desktop and switch it off; for VNC, close or uninstall the VNC program.
If you do use it: make sure the account has a strong, unique password.
Never make it reachable from the internet (for example with router 'port forwarding'); use a VPN instead.

protect_databases.title: Protect the database on this device
protect_databases.why: Databases hold data directly. Many are installed with no password or allow every device on the network to connect.
steps: Find which program installed the database (often a home-server app or a developer tool).
In the database's settings, set a strong password and allow connections only from the device itself ('localhost') unless other devices really need it.
If you don't know why it is there, ask whoever set up the device, or uninstall the program that added it.

secure_cameras.title: Secure your camera's video stream
secure_cameras.why: Some cameras let anyone on the network watch their video, or use a default password that is easy to find online.
steps: Open the camera's app or settings page and change any default password.
Look for 'RTSP', 'ONVIF' or 'Local streaming'. Switch it off if you only use the maker's app, or make sure it needs a password.
Update the camera's software (firmware) from its app.

secure_smart_home.title: Add a password (and encryption) to smart-home messages
secure_smart_home.why: Unprotected MQTT lets any device on your network read sensors or switch things on and off.
steps: Open the settings of your smart-home hub or MQTT broker (for example Home Assistant's Mosquitto add-on).
Turn off 'anonymous' access and create a username and password for your devices.
If possible, use the encrypted port 8883 (MQTT over TLS) instead of 1883.

keep_devices_updated.title: Keep the device's software up to date
keep_devices_updated.why: Updates fix security problems that attackers know about. Many network services are only risky on old versions.
steps: Computers: turn on automatic updates (Windows Update, macOS Software Update).
Routers, cameras, printers and network storage: open the device's app or settings page and look for 'Firmware update' or 'Check for updates'.
Replace devices that no longer get updates from their maker.

review_unknown_service.title: Check what this service is
review_unknown_service.why: An unexpected service isn't necessarily a problem, but every service that accepts connections is a possible way in, so it's worth knowing what each one is.
steps: Note the device and port number shown in LanWatch.
Check the device's settings page or app, or search the web for the device model and port number, to find out what uses it.
If it is a feature you don't use, switch it off. If you can't tell what it is, ask whoever set up the device.
